# Cleaning a dirty Excel sheet {#sec-clean}

```{r}
#| label: setup-clean
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
load_steps("code/1_clean_data.r", "clean")
```

Real clinic data arrive as a spreadsheet typed by several people over two years. I make a realistic one on purpose, so that every cleaning step has something to fix.

The script is `code/1_clean_data.r`. It turns the sheet into one tidy row per patient per visit.

## Where the dirty sheet comes from

A small Python script reads the wide CSV from chapter 1 and makes it dirty. It adds mixed date formats, Buddhist Era years, Thai month names, many spellings of each category, mmol/L typed into a mg/dL column, units typed into cells, missing-value codes, a mistyped year and duplicate rows. It is shown here and not run, because the Excel file is already in the repository.

```{python}
#| label: dirty-generator
#| eval: false
#| file: data/_source/make_dirty_fbs.py
```

## Step 1: packages, paths and lookups

The script opens with the packages, two paths and three small lookups. The lookups hold what I know about the mess in advance, namely the text that means "no value", the Thai month abbreviations and the date the study closed.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-1
#| message: false
```

## Step 2: import the sheet as text

Almost every column mixes numbers with words, so I do not let readxl guess. I read the whole sheet as text and give each variable its type later, in a step I can see.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-2
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(df, 8)
```

The sheet has `r nrow(df)` rows and `r ncol(df)` columns. Some of these rows are duplicates and some cells hold units or words, which the next steps deal with.

## Step 3: clean the patient id

The patient number was typed in three styles. Keeping only the digits turns all of them into one integer.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-3
```

## Step 4: drop duplicate records

First I drop the records entered twice, identical in every field. Some patients can still appear twice with one value typed differently. The file alone cannot say which entry is right, so the rule is to keep the first record. The message names the patients, so the data collector can check the paper form.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-4
```

The message names `r length(dup_id)` such `r ifelse(length(dup_id) == 1, "patient", "patients")`, with id `r paste(dup_id, collapse = ", ")`. After this step `r nrow(df)` patients remain, one row each.

## Step 5: put every free text field on one spelling

I squish the spaces and lower the case before writing any rule. Then " M ", "m" and "MALE" are already one thing.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-5
```

## Step 6: treatment arm

Every spelling of the arm ends in the letter of the arm, so one pattern covers them all.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-6
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
table(df$treatment, useNA = "ifany")
```

## Step 7: sex

Sex was typed as numbers, letters and words in two languages. Each group of spellings maps to one level.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-7
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
table(df$sex, useNA = "ifany")
```

## Step 8: age, BMI and diabetes duration become numbers

Units were typed beside the numbers. `parse_number()` keeps the number and drops the rest.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-8
```

## Step 9: impossible values

Some values cannot be true. I keep the offending patients in an object first, so their ids can be reported before the values are changed. A lost decimal point can be repaired, but a missing code becomes missing.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-9
```

`r nrow(bad_baseline)` patients had an impossible baseline value.

## Step 10: wide to long, one row per visit

A mixed model needs one row per visit. `pivot_longer()` splits each column name into the variable and the month in one move.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-10
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(dfl, 8)
```

The data now have `r nrow(dfl)` rows, which is `r dplyr::n_distinct(dfl$id)` patients with five planned visits each.

## Step 11: drop the visits that never happened

A visit with neither a date nor an FBS value is a patient who stopped coming. That is dropout and not dirt, so the row goes and the mixed model handles the gap later.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-11
```

`r nrow(dfl)` visits remain.

## Step 12: FBS becomes a number on one unit

The glucometer shows mmol/L and the lab reports mg/dL, and staff typed both into one column. The size of the number tells the unit, because no fasting sugar in mg/dL is below 30 and none in mmol/L is above 30.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-12
```

`r nrow(fbs_fixed)` values were converted or set to missing.

## Step 13: visit dates, one habit per line

Dates came in five habits, namely day first, ISO, an Excel serial number, Buddhist Era years and Thai month names. Each line of this step fixes exactly one habit and leaves the text ready for the next line. After the step, look at `date` and `txt` side by side. That comparison is the whole lesson.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-13
```

`r nrow(date_bad)` visit `r ifelse(nrow(date_bad) == 1, "date", "dates")` could not be used.

## Step 14: time since the first visit

Month 3 is the plan, but the real visit can be a few days early or late. I count the actual days and calendar months from each patient's first visit, so the mixed model can use either the planned month or the exact time.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-14
```

`r nrow(off_window)` visits fell more than 21 days from their due date. Zero is the good result here, because the simulated visits were all within 14 days of their due date. The check stays in the script because real clinics are rarely so tidy. When no visit is flagged, the message ends with an empty id list.

Only the variables the analysis needs are kept, in a sensible order.

The check compares the cleaned data with what I know from the simulation. If a cleaning rule were wrong, one of these numbers would no longer match and the script would stop.

```{r}
#| label: clean-step-16
```

The cleaned data hold `r dplyr::n_distinct(dfl$id)` patients and `r nrow(dfl)` visits, the same as the simulation produced after dropout.
